sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Gold is known currently as the most active single-element electrocatlayst for CO2 electroreduction reaction (CRR) to CO. In this work, we combine Au with a second metal element, Cu, to reduce the amount of precious metal content by increasing a surface-to-mass ratio, and to achieve comparable activity to Au-based catalysts. In particular, we demonstrate that the introduction of Au-Cu bi-functional “interface” is more beneficial than a simple and conventional homogeneous alloying of Au and Cu in stabilizing the key intermediate species, *COOH. Main advantages of the proposed metal-metal bi-functional interfacial catalyst over the bimetallic alloys include that 1) utilization of active materials is improved, and 2) intrinsic properties of metals are less affected in bi-functional catalysts than in alloys, which can then facilitate a rational bi-functional design. These results demonstrate for the first time the importance of metal-metal interfaces and morphology, rather than the simple mixing of the two metals homogeneously, for enhanced catalytic synergies.
INTRODUCTION
Page 2 of 24

As a clean and carbon-neutral technology, a considerable interest has been focused on the CO2 electroreduction reaction (CRR) since it can convert global-warming CO2 gas to fuels and chemicals.1 At the same time, the CRR technology serves as an energy carrier to circumvent an intermittent supply of renewable energies such as solar and wind powers. The main challenge of the CRR, however, is to develop catalysts which satisfy three conditions; 1) high activity to reduce significant overpotentials required to prompt the electroreduction reactions, 2) high selectivity to produce a desired single product without losing Faradaic efficiency and complicated post-separation processes, and 3) low catalyst cost to be applicable for a mass production. At present, no catalysts fulfilling all three conditions have been developed.
Among various CO2 reduction products, carbon monoxide (CO) is one of the simplest and yet most useful chemical feedstocks since it can be further converted into liquid fuels via wellestablished Fischer-Tropsch process when combined with H2. Theoretical analysis on transition metal catalysts showed that the activity of the CRR to CO is usually limited by a formation of *COOH (* denotes a adsorbed species on catalysts),2 in which the active catalysts should bind *COOH strongly enough to lower the energy requirement for this reaction. In addition, the catalysts should bind *CO weakly enough to desorb CO off from the catalyst surface easily without undergoing further protonations to undesired products. A competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) should be considered as well since it lowers current densities for the CRR.3-4 Due to a scaling relation, however, the binding strengths of *COOH and *H often go parallel with that of *CO (Figure 2)5, and it is difficult to meet all three criteria simultaneously if a single metal element is used. Thus, a preferential and independent stabilization of particular reaction intermediates by breaking the conventional scaling relation has been the main challenge for the catalyst developments in the CRR.

Recent theoretical and experimental studies have shown that Au is the most active single element CRR catalyst to produce CO.5-6 For further performance improvements, the nanostructured Au, e.g., oxygen plasma-induced Au islands7, oxide-derived Au8, Au nanowires9, and Au nanoparticles10 have been introduced to exhibit increased CRR current densities with reduced overpotentials and a high selectivity for CO over H2 gas. Despite the exciting progress shown in these efforts in the performance enhancements, however, the use of Au as a practical CRR catalyst is still significantly hindered due to its high price, prompting a need for new catalysts with a comparable activity to Au-based catalyst but with a significantly reduced amount of Au.
In various catalytic reactions, homogeneous alloying is a general strategy to increase the catalytic activity and to reduce the use of noble metals such as Au and Pt.11-14 Kim et al showed that alloyed Au3Cu1 nanoparticle electrochemically catalyze CO2 to produce CO with higher specific activity than Au nanoparticle catalyst.14 Recently, Hansen et al reported CO2 and CO electroreduction alloy catalysts with an A3B composition, which break the scaling relation by stabilizing the particular reaction intermediates such as *COOH and *CHO preferentially. The reduced overpotential in A3B alloys originates from the binding configuration of adsorbates, where both *CHO and *COOH bind through both C and O atoms, while *CO binds through only C atom. Therefore, alloys that bind the O end in *CHO and *COOH strongly could stabilize *CHO and *COOH over *CO. However, it is noteworthy that, although the binding strengths of alloys generally lie between those of constituting alloying elements, sometimes the binding behaviors of alloys exhibits unexpected characteristics 4, 14-16 which is in part because the electronic structure (such as the d-band center) of the component metals gets modified significantly when they are alloyed. This makes a rational design of bi-functional alloy catalyst

rather difficult due to unpredictable properties of these homogeneously mixed alloys. In this sense, it would be desirable to combine two metals with their intrinsic properties more or less preserved in a bi-functional catalyst so that the well-established knowledge on pure metals such as the binding affinities for certain elements can be used and controlled to choose the metal candidates in designing a bi-functional catalyst.
Scheme 1. Exploiting strategy to preferentially stabilize *COOH by introducing bi-functional effects. In this case, metal A and B correspond to Au and Cu, respectively.
In this work, to reduce the amount of precious metal (Au) significantly as well as to achieve an activity comparable to the Au catalyst by introducing the bi-functional synergistic effects, we combine Au with oxygen-affinitive second metal element to create a bimetallic interface rather than alloys. Among fcc metals (Ag, Au, Cu, Ir, Ni, Pd, Pt, Rh) considered in the previous studies for the CRR, Ag, Pd and Pt are not affinitive for O, while Ir, Ni and Rh are too affinitive for O that would result in the surface poisoning by the *OH species.5 In addition, Ir, Ni, Pd, Pt, and Rh all bind *CO so strongly that they prevent the CO desorption, whereas Ag binds *C-species comparatively weakly to Au, thus inactive for the formation of *COOH. Thus, we chose Cu as the most suitable metal for seeking the bi-functional effects with Au since it binds *COOH/*CO

moderately but binds *O more strongly than Au for the further stabilization of *COOH through the oxygen-metal interaction as shown in Scheme 1.
COMPUTATIONAL DETAILS Electronic energies were calculated with the RPBE exchange functional17-18 using projectoraugmented wave pseudopotential19 by the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP).20-21 We modeled the (111) surface using a four-layered slab of (3×3) surface unit cell and a three-layered slab of (4×4) surface unit cell for the pure metal surfaces and bulk alloys (Cu3Au1 and Au3Cu1), respectively. The bimetallic interface is modeled by a Au-island on Cu, where a monolayer of Au-island is placed on a three-layered Cu (111) surface. In all cases, the adsorbates and the upper two layers were relaxed until the residual force is less than 0.05 eV/Å, while atoms in the bottom layers were fixed to their bulk positions. K-points were sampled using the 3×3×1 and 2×2×1 Monkhorst-Pack mesh for the pure metal surfaces and the bulk alloys, respectively.22 For large Au-island models, only the gamma point was used. The plane-wave cutoff energy of 500 eV was used for all geometry optimizations. The binding energies of adsorbates were calculated as EB[*X] = E[*X] – E[*] – E[X], where E[*X] and E[*] denote calculated electronic energies of various surfaces with and without adsorbate X, respectively, and E[X] is calculated electronic energy of molecule X in the 10 Å × 10 Å × 10 Å box.
We performed two primary tests to appropriately model the Au-island on Cu. Firstly, to determine the size of a surface unit cell required to avoid an imaginary interaction between consecutive periodic Au-island images, we calculated EB[*CO] and EB[*COOH] at the corner site of (3×3) Au on various sizes of Cu substrate from (5×5) to (7×7). The result indicates that the interaction becomes negligible when the distance between two Au images is as far as 10 Å.

Based on this result, next, to see the convergence of the size of Au island on Cu, we again calculated EB[*CO] and EB[*COOH] on various sizes of Au-island from (2×2) (on the (5×5) Cuhost) to (4×4) (on the (7×7) Cu-host). The (3×3) Au-island on the (6×6) Cu-host showed a nearly converged result for EB[*CO] and EB[*COOH] (around 0.05 eV difference compared to the larger model) while minimizing the computational cost (Table S1). This island (or interfacial) model is then compared with another morphology of the Au-Cu bimetallic system, i.e., an alloy. Two stoichiometric compositions of the Au-Cu alloy, Cu3Au1 and Au3Cu1, are considered. All considered models are shown in Figure 1.
We note that Au-overlayer (or Au-skin) on Cu host is shown to be unstable due to a large lattice mismatch between Au (4.08 Å) and Cu (3.61 Å), resulting in a significantly distorted geometry of Au overlayer. This indicates that the formation of Au-island rather than the Au-thin layer covering the extensive area of Cu surface is more plausible. To investigate a stability of Au island, we compared a relative stability of (3×6) Au island and two-layered (3×3) Au island on the Cu substrate, where the two dimensional Au island, the former, is more stable than the three dimensional Au island, the latter, by more than 3 eV (Fig. S1.). This shows that the formation of two dimensional Au island is preferred to the three dimensional Au island, supporting that the considered one-layer island model is reasonable.
All conventional binding sites, i.e., atop, bridge, fcc-hollow and hcp-hollow sites, were considered and various bi-functional binding sites (binding through both Au and Cu) were also considered for the bulk alloys and Au-island models. The most stable binding sites and their energies are then used for further analysis (Fig. S2.). To convert electronic energies into free energies, free energy corrections and solvation effects should be added. Zero-point energy, enthalpy and entropy corrections were calculated using the harmonic oscillator approximation

with all degrees of freedoms displaced by 0.01 Å with a temperature set to 298.15 K. For molecules (CO2, CO, H2O), an ideal-gas method was used to obtain free energies with pressures set to 101,325 Pa for CO2 and CO and a fugacity set to 3,534 Pa for H2O. We used an approximate solvation correction to account for the effect of water, where *COOH and *CO are stabilized by 0.25 and 0.1 eV, respectively.2 Free energy diagrams were established using the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) method, which assumes a free energy of protonelectron pair equivalent to a half of free energy of gaseous hydrogen at standard condition, i.e., µ(H++e-) = 0.5µ(H2). 23 In this method, potential dependent free energy of proton-electron pair is evaluated as µ(H++e−) = 0.5µ(H2) – eU, where U is the applied potential. The CHE model allows to estimate the catalyst performance according to the required potential to make all elementary electrochemical reactions thermodynamically downhill. This potential (so called “limiting potential (UL)”) is defined as UL = −∆GMAX/e, where ∆GMAX is the largest energy barrier among elementary electrochemical reactions. The intermediate reaction step with ∆GMAX is a potential determining step (PDS), and is a thermodynamic bottleneck of the entire CO2 electroreduction reaction. More computational details can be found in our previous publications.4, 24 We note that the calculated limiting potential matches well with the experimental onset potential,2 and, in many cases, the thermodynamic limiting potential reasonably estimated the catalytic trend.25-26

sections.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS
sections.text:
To facilitate the CO2 reduction reaction and to prevent the H2 evolution reaction, the following three criteria should be satisfied; i) catalysts should bind *COOH strongly to promote the CO2 activation, ii) catalysts should bind *H weakly to hinder the *H adsorption, iii) catalysts should bind *CO weakly to remove the produced CO and regenerate the catalytic active sites.

sections.heading: PDS.
sections.text:
We plotted the free energy diagrams for CO2 reduction reaction in Figure 2. We first compare the catalytic properties of Au, Cu, and its bimetallic alloys (Au3Cu1 and Cu3Au1). Our calculations indicate that the free energy change (∆G) to form *COOH systematically decrease as the Cu contents increase from Au to Au3Cu1 and Cu3Au1 (Figure 2). Counter-intuitively, free energy change (∆G) to form *COOH at Cu3Au1 and Au3Cu1 are smaller than the Cu, indicating that the binding affinities of Cu3Au1 and Au3Cu1 are not between those of their parent elements, Au and Cu. Au3Cu1 (0.72 eV) and Cu3Au1 (0.69 eV) have smaller ∆G’s for the PDS of CRR than Au (1.20 eV) and Cu (0.94 eV), resulting in an easier activation of CO2 (Figure 2A). Similarly, the ∆G’s for the PDS of HER on Au3Cu1 (0.33 eV) and Cu3Au1 (0.02 eV) are smaller than Au (0.54 eV), indicating that hydrogen production is also more facile on the Au/Cu bulk alloys than on pure Au (Figure 2B).

To grasp relative activity of H2 evolution reaction vs. CO2 reduction reaction for the considered catalysts based on the calculated thermodynamic barriers, the UL(HER) is plotted versus UL(CRR) in Figure 3. These calculated results (for Au, Cu, Cu3Au1, and Au3Cu1) agree well with a previous study by Kim et al which compared the CRR activity and selectivity for Au, Cu and their alloyed nanoparticles.14 It was observed that the turnover rate for CO production was the largest with the Au3Cu1 nanoparticle followed by Au, AuCu, Cu3Au1, and Cu. The faradaic efficiency for H2 increased as the Cu content in the alloyed nanoparticle increases (40~60% for Cu and Cu3Au1), lowering the selectivity toward CO. Such a high faradaic efficiency for H2 is attributed to the very less negative UL (HER) for Cu3Au1 and Cu. On the other hand, for Au and Au3Cu1, the UL (HER) is more negative than that for Cu3Au1 and Cu, which accounts for the smaller faradaic efficiency for H2.
Figure 3. The calculated limiting potential for HER plotted versus that for CRR. As the arrows indicate, less negative UL(CRR) (right region) and UL(HER) (upper region) denote high activity for CRR and HER, respectively. Corner and bi-functional sites of the Au-i@Cu are considered,

We next focus on the results for the Au-island on Cu catalysts (Au-i@Cu). The Au-i@Cu appears to be a good catalyst since it has a lower free energy barrier (0.73 eV and 0.60 eV for the corner and bi-functional sites, respectively) for the adsorption of *COOH than various adsorption sites of most active Au (1.20 eV for the (111) surface, 0.70 eV for the (211) edge, and 0.62 eV for the corner site)24, while it has a high free energy barrier (0.38 eV) for the adsorption of *H comparable to Au (0.54 eV for the (111) surface, 0.25 eV for the (211) edge, and 0.58 eV for the corner site). As the free energy change of *CO desorption (*CO *+CO) at the Au-i@Cu is only 0.19 eV, while that of the further protonation of *CO to *CHO (*CO+H++e- *CHO) is 0.72 eV, we expect that *CO be easily desorbed as produced. Interestingly, Figure 3 shows that Au-i@Cu is more active for CRR than the Au3Cu1, Cu3Au1 and the Au edge sites, but also less active for HER, increasing the net CRR selectivity further.24 In the next section, we discuss the origin of enhanced CRR performance of Au-i@Cu compared to the corresponding alloy counterparts.
Discussion on the CRR activity of Au-i@Cu To understand and assess the bi-functional effect at the bimetallic alloys and Au-i@Cu, we systematically investigated the binding geometries and energies of *COOH on Au, Au3Cu1 and Au-i@Cu, since the strong binding of *COOH leads to the reduction of the UL for the CRR (Figure 4).

We first note that the *COOH binding energy on Au3Cu1 (111) is stronger than that on Au (111) by 0.48 eV primarily due to an alloying with Cu. This indicates that alloying Au with more oxygen affinitive Cu indeed helps to stabilize *COOH, as expected from a bi-functional design, which is in agreement with the previous theoretical studies.5, 13 It is noticeable that C in *COOH binds to Au, while O in *COOH binds to Cu on the Au3Cu1. For comparison, the opposite binding configuration (O-Au and C-Cu bindings) indeed yielded a 0.25 eV weaker binding. The C-Au and O-Au distances in Au (111) being longer than those of C-Au and O-Cu bonds in Au3Cu1 are in line with the calculated binding energies (Fig. 4A and 4B). When an edge site of Au3Cu1 is utilized for CRR, the under-coordination effects can improve the activity as evidenced by pure Au case.24 However, we note that the under-coordination effects for Au3Cu1 are not helpful to enhance the CRR activity (Supporting Information).
We now discuss the origin of activity improvement for Au-i@Cu. In Figure 4E, we decomposed the free energy contribution of PDS (CO2+H ++e- *COOH) into two components, the under-coordination and the bi-functional effects. We also plotted for the case of Au-i@Au as a comparison. When changing from Au (111) to the corner site of Au-i@Au or Au-i@Cu, the under-coordination effects stabilize *COOH by 0.69 and 0.47 eV, respectively. As *COOH binding site changes from the corner site to the bi-functional site, *COOH on Au-i@Cu is further stabilized by 0.13 eV, while such binding site on Au-i@Au does not stabilize *COOH due to an absence of the bi-functional effects. For Au-i@Cu, the C-Au distances in both binding configurations (corner site vs. bi-functional site) are similar, while the O-Cu distance in a bifunctional site is shorter than the O-Au distance in a corner site, consistent with the binding energies.

A wide variety of metal alloys have been employed in the literature to improve the catalytic activity by fine-tuning the binding energies of adsorbates (e.g., EB[*CO], EB[*O] and EB[*H] for CRR, ORR and HER, respectively).4, 13, 27-32 The key aspect of metal alloys to control the adsorbate binding energies is linked to the changes in the d-band center (Dc), which is an informative measure for the binding strength of reaction intermediates.33 We assume that metals partially lose their intrinsic properties when two metals are alloyed, thus the d-band center of alloy changes from that of pure metals. Figure 5 shows the density of states and the calculated dband centers for the Au3Cu1, Cu3Au1 and Au-i@Cu compared to the pure Au and Cu. The results

On the other hand, the electronic structures of the constituting elements in Aui@Cu were less affected than those of the alloys. Similar trends were seen for the Au island on different substrates with different binding affinity; Au-i@Ir and Au-i@Pt, for which the binding energies of Au island on Ir and Pt are stronger than on Cu by 2 eV (Table S2. and Fig. S5.), indicate that the metal-metal interface can roughly preserve the electronic properties of pure metal better than the homogeneous alloy mixing. This bi-functional “interface” makes a rational bi-metallic catalyst design easier since one can then systematically exploit the well-established knowledge for pure metals to control the stability of desired intermediates in a bi-metallic catalyst in a predictable manner.

Along with the enhanced CRR activity, we expect that the Au-i@Cu reduce the amount of Au compared to the Au-based catalyst since, for catalytic reactions, only surface atoms are utilized, thus a high surface-to-mass ratio leads to the reduction of the catalyst cost. It might be helpful to consider possible experimental techniques which would enable a synthesis of the Au-i@Cu catalysts proposed in this work. The vapor deposition techniques have been applied to form metal islands on the substrate and the resultant islands were characterized by a scanning tunneling microscopy (STM).36-37 A precise control of the metal island coverage is also possible by controlling the deposition time at a constant deposition rate. We believe that by changing the amount of deposited Au on Cu, the optimal amount of Au can be determined to maximize both its catalytic activity for CRR and effectiveness of manufacturing cost.

sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we proposed the metal-metal interface catalyst to obtain a comparable activity for the CRR compared to Au catalysts with the maximized surface-to-mass ratio to reduce the catalyst cost. By comparing free energy change for the *COOH adsorption, we found that both bulk alloy (Au3Cu1) and the Au-i@Cu stabilize *COOH due to the bi-functional effects of oxygen affinitive Cu, yet the *COOH is further stabilized on the Au-i@Cu by the under-

coordination effects. However, the under-coordination effects are not helpful to improve the CRR activity for Au3Cu1. We then examined the DOS and the d-band center of two types of catalysts, and found that the shape of DOS and the d-band center changed considerably for the alloys, while the changes were insignificant for the Au-i@Cu. This confirms our hypothesis that the alloying changes the intrinsic electronic properties, while introducing the metal-metal interface roughly preserve their own electronic properties. We expect our approach be particularly beneficial and intuitive as it enables a rational bi-metallic catalyst design through the well-established knowledge for pure metals.
